Talsmag aInternational Food Policy Research Institute, United States bBetter Diets and Nutrition CGIAR Science Program, Kenya cDevelopment Impact Group, World Bank, United States dNational Institute of Nutrition, Viet Nam eSight and Life, Rwanda fDepartment of Nutrition and Dietetics, University of Ibadan, Nigeria gDivision of Human Nutrition and Health, Wageningen University and Research, the Netherlands hInternational Food Policy Research Institute, Division of Human Nutrition and Health, Wageningen University and Research, the Netherlands A B S T R A C T Although fruits are an important part of healthy diets, they are relatively expensive, so most individuals consume less than recommended. We use a randomized control trial to study a voucher program designed to improve the affordability of fruits in peri-urban and urban settings in Vietnam and Nigeria, and analyze whether vouchers can increase fruit consumption. The trial took place in 2021 among 601 households in Vietnam and 611 households in Nigeria. Vouchers were distributed between March and July in Vietnam and between June and November in Nigeria. In both contexts, a large majority of consumers who received vouchers used them. Following project conclusion, we find suggestive evidence of sustained increased fruit consumption only in Vietnam. In Nigeria, vouchers increased consumption of certain fruit categories during program implementation, but we find no evidence of sustained impacts. Fruit consumption is higher across the board in Vietnam, and the sample is wealthier overall, suggesting fruit affordability may not be a binding constraint for consumption. In Nigeria, the increase in consumption during the program along with a post-project decline suggest a lack of household resources to sustain consumption once the project concluded. The results suggest vouchers can improve consumption of healthy foods like fruits, but other actions are needed to make them more affordable in the longer term. 1. JSON: Name: fruit_voucher_rct_pipeline Title: Randomized controlled trial evaluation of weekly fruit vouchers to increase household fruit consumption in urban and peri-urban Nigeria and Vietnam Short Hypothesis: Provision of weekly, non-transferable vouchers redeemable for selected fruits causes an increase in household fruit consumption and household expenditures on voucher-targeted fruits during the intervention period relative to no voucher. Related Work: Prior work has tested price-based incentives and subsidies for healthier foods in high-income settings and a few LMIC programs, and has compared in-kind or targeted subsidies to cash transfers. Existing randomized or quasi-experimental evaluations report mixed results: some show short-term increases in fruit and vegetable purchases while others find little or no sustained diet-quality improvements. Limitations across studies include small or underpowered samples, short follow-up windows that preclude assessment of persistence, reliance on self-reported intake without administrative redemption data, limited study of heterogeneity by baseline affordability or wealth, and insufficient attention to substitution between subsidized and non-subsidized items. There is also sparse causal evidence from urban LMIC contexts on voucher size effects, vendor compliance, and whether voucher-induced changes persist after program end. Abstract: This pipeline describes a reproducible research plan to estimate causal impacts of weekly, non-transferable fruit vouchers on household fruit consumption in urban and peri-urban sites in Nigeria and Vietnam using a randomized controlled trial with two voucher sizes and a no-voucher control. The approach combines administrative voucher redemption records, repeated short monitoring surveys during implementation, and two post-intervention endlines to estimate intent-to-treat effects on (i) types of voucher-targeted fruits consumed (24-hour and 7-day recalls), (ii) expenditures on voucher and non-voucher fruits, and (iii) aggregate dietary diversity (continuous MDD-W) and potential substitution away from vegetables. Main contributions are (a) rigorous identification of short-run and post-program effects using randomized voucher magnitude, (b) linkage of administrative redemption to self-reported consumption to validate take-up, and (c) heterogeneity and attrition-robust analyses by baseline consumption and asset-wealth. Expected outcomes are precise estimates of short-term increases in voucher-fruit consumption and evidence on whether effects persist conditional on baseline affordability. Experiments: Datasets: baseline household survey, five monitoring rounds (including two during voucher roll-out), two post-intervention in-person endlines, administrative voucher redemption logs, vendor enrollment records. Sample: randomized 3-arm panel (control, small voucher, large voucher) with stratification by neighborhood, baseline fruit consumption tercile, and replacement status; target N ≈ 600 households per country. Primary outcomes: (1) count of voucher-target fruit categories consumed (0–3) in 24h and 7d recalls; (2) household expenditures on voucher fruits (local currency) in last 7 days; (3) continuous MDD-W score (0–10). Secondary outcomes: counts/expenditures for non-voucher fruits, vegetable counts/expenditures, total food expenditures, voucher redemption rate. Baselines: no-voucher control; internal comparison between small vs large voucher arms. Estimators: intent-to-treat OLS with stratification-cell fixed effects, household-clustered robust SEs; Poisson/negative-binomial for counts; FWER-adjusted p-values for multiple outcomes; Lee (bounds) for differential attrition; LASSO-selected covariate robustness checks. Experimental setup: pre-specify primary outcomes and analysis code; run country-specific and pooled analyses; evaluate redemption fidelity using administrative logs. Ablation and comparisons: (A) size-ablation: compare small vs large voucher effects to estimate dose-response; (B) component-ablation: restrict sample to households with no exposure to accessibility/acceptability components and compare to full sample to isolate voucher-only effects; (C) timing-ablation: estimate effects during intervention (monitoring rounds) versus post-intervention (endlines) to measure persistence. Power analyses: report minimum detectable effects for primary outcomes given sample and observed variance; pre-register all hypotheses. Risk Factors and Limitations: Attrition and differential survey nonresponse across arms can bias estimates; COVID-related disruptions or distribution errors can reduce effective treatment exposure. Self-reported consumption and expenditure measures are subject to recall and social-desirability bias; administrative voucher logs can miss unrecorded redemptions if vendors fail to comply. Seasonal variation in fruit availability and prices can confound short-run versus post-intervention comparisons. External validity is limited to urban and peri-urban contexts and to the specific fruits selected for vouchers. Statistical power may be insufficient to detect small persistent effects or to estimate heterogeneous effects in subgroups. Spillovers within communities (sharing or resale of vouchers) can attenuate intent-to-treat estimates. General equilibrium effects on local fruit prices or vendor behavior are possible but not measured comprehensively.
